Rethinking Local News: How Sarah Alvarez Is Building Journalism in Support of Community Needs

Nieman Reports · 2026-11-11 13:00 UTC

Sarah Alvarez has spent much of her career rethinking how local journalism can serve the public. After working as a civil rights attorney, then as a reporter and producer at the NPR station Michigan Public, she founded Outlier Media in 2016. Alvarez said the Detroit-based nonprofit newsroom was designed to fill information and accountability gaps in communities that were often overlooked by traditional news organizations.. One of its signature innovations, TXT OUTLIER, is a text message service Alvarez created to connect Detroiters directly with journalists and provide practical information on issues affecting their lives, from utility bills to housing and foreclosures. Under Alvarez’s leadership, Outlier also expanded its Documenters program, an initiative that trains and pays residents to attend and report on public meetings to create a public record of local government decisions in places that don’t have press coverage. The initiative has engaged more than 700 Detroiters and since spread nationwide, creating new opportunities for civic participation and public accountability.

What to Watch for in the 2026 U.S. Midterms

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC

With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

India Targets Journalists in Crackdown on Growing Protest Movement

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-19 21:20 UTC

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

Testing the Legal Limits of Press Access

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-15 14:51 UTC

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. This Newsroom Wants You to Be Part of the Journey Before It Even Starts

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-06 10:00 UTC

My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

America’s Shrinking Local Newsrooms, Through a Photographer’s Lens

Nieman Reports · 2026-10-02 12:30 UTC

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

The Paper 澎湃新闻 · 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Human Rights Watch Mourns Death of Activist Nabeel Rajab

Human Rights Watch · 2026-11-18 21:23 UTC

Click to expand Image Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab arrives for his appeal hearing at court in Manama, February 11, 2015. © 2015 Hamad I Mohammed/Reuters (New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack. Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded and later became the president of the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights. Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies

Human Rights Watch · 2026-11-18 17:09 UTC

Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades. Click to expand Image Former Central African Republic Prime Minister Nicolas Tiangaye in Bangui, January 8, 2014. © 2014 Eric Feferberg/AFP via Getty Images Tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup. For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president. In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

Click to expand Image Baktybek Moldaliev. © Private Moldaliev, 49, who worked as a welder, and commented regularly on politics on Facebook was first detained for a day in November 2025, when police seized his phone as evidence and gained access to it, according to his wife, Elvira Zhusupova. Six months later in May 2026 Moldaliev was charged with inciting "mass unrest"—vague charges frequently brought against social media users in Kyrgyzstan who are prosecuted for sharing or resharing content online. He was taken into custody where he has remained since. After a month and a half, authorities changed the charges to the production and distribution of extremist materials.

Mergers and European competitiveness: Evidence on innovation and market power

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-19 00:00 UTC

Europe’s competitiveness debate has renewed calls to give greater weight to scale, investment, and efficiencies in merger policy. This column presents evidence from mergers reviewed by the European Commission between 1990 and 2024. On average, markups and profits rise following mergers, while citation-weighted patenting falls for both merging firms and their rivals. The responses of rival firms are particularly informative for distinguishing firm-specific rationalisation from a broader weakening of competitive pressure.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

The health costs of organised crime

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-19 00:00 UTC

Organised crime can impose costs that extend well beyond violence, market distortions, and weakened institutions. This column presents evidence on the long-run health consequences of illegal toxic-waste disposal in Southern Italy. Comparing municipalities similarly close to illegal disposal sites but differentially exposed because of historical wind patterns shows large and persistent effects on the number of cancer deaths in downwind municipalities. Consistent with epidemiological evidence on dioxin exposure, these effects emerge only after long latencies. Effects are particularly pronounced on deaths from all causes among younger age groups.

Resilience without retreat: How EU firms are redesigning their supply chains

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-18 00:00 UTC

Geopolitical tensions are changing the nature of supply-chain risk. This column presents new survey evidence showing that EU firms increasingly regard trade disruptions as persistent but are moving away from emergency responses such as stockpiling towards longer-term diversification of suppliers and markets. The EU Single Market provides an important buffer against external shocks. At the same time, experimental evidence shows that geopolitical disruptions can have sizeable and asymmetric effects on firms' investment.

Gradually, then suddenly – the fiscal value of climate resilience

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-18 00:00 UTC

The human and economic costs of extreme weather events are already large and will grow as temperatures rise further. This column argues that, seen through the lens of the sovereign balance sheet rather than the budget, adaptation reduces the expected fiscal cost of physical climate risk – and the case for investing in it becomes clear.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

European funds often fall short on currency hedging

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-18 00:00 UTC

The theory of optimal currency hedging has been well established for decades. This column uses new regulatory data to analyse how 2,806 European investment funds use currency forwards and swaps and how the use compares to theoretical benchmarks. It finds that only a minority follow hedging policies close to the portfolio-theory benchmark, and observed derivative trading does not significantly contribute to lower fund risk. Yet a feasible optimal strategy could lower volatility by about 10%, at very modest additional transaction cost.

newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

The geography of financial frictions

CEPR VoxEU · 2026-11-17 00:00 UTC

Firms’ access to external finance differs widely across Europe. This column uses data from the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises to map these differences and to study what they mean for monetary policy. The authors find that countries in which firms face tighter financial frictions respond less to the ECB’s monetary policy changes, and that they face a worse trade-off between output and inflation. A model of the monetary union suggests that financial integration in the spirit of the Savings and Investments Union would make monetary policy more effective, but potentially at a cost to financial stability.

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences -- by Pierre Bachas, Christopher A. Hoy, Anders Jensen, Mahvish Shaukat

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy -- by Bruce C. Greenwald, Joseph E. Stiglitz

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

We use the Phelps-Winter customer market—providing a better theory of price determination for large parts of the economy than the standard model—to show that raising interest rates induces higher prices, as firms value current profits more, and are more willing to lose customers for short-term gains. These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement -- by Emanuele Colonnelli, Timothy McQuade, Natalia Rigol, Benjamin N. Roth

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Gambling for Goals -- by Costas Arkolakis, Spencer Y. Kwon, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, Hyunjoo Yang

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Young adults in advanced economies have grown more pessimistic about their economic prospects in recent years. At the same time, gambling-like financial activities have proliferated. We link these trends through a Friedman-Savage (1948) motive: when life goals such as homeownership or marriage seem out of reach, individuals turn to financial gambles. We test this theory using an original survey combined with millions of linked records from Korea’s leading credit bureau, telecom provider, and credit card issuer. Consistent with the theory, individuals who place greater importance on hard-to-reach goals take more risk, and the form of risk they take varies systematically with their distance from those goals. Within individuals, cryptocurrency app usage rises during unemployment and falls after winning the right to purchase price-regulated housing through a lottery. A calibration shows how hard-to-reach goals lead households to act more aggressively on their beliefs, amplifying the consequences of overoptimism.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability -- by Jitendra Aswani, Roberto Rigobon

NBER · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 16% (structural estimates). These effects are confined to non-financial firms; for financial firms, governance adoption alone is in-sufficient, as sustainable loan borrowers environmental performance does not improve. Firms with stronger environmental performance are less likely to adopt sustainable governance. Results are robust to alternative definitions and extensive specification checks.

institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

TLDR Starting on October 1st, 2026, many of Astra’s tool calls in my personal workflow that included free text exhibited the removal of spaces, for example turning “correct 120/120” into “correct120/120”. This has been observed by others, including in other OpenAI models, such as Sol. This never organically occurred in the main chat, and never occurred in any Claude model over the same time frame. It mainly arose partway through sessions, and once it happened it could continue for an extended period of time. It was easy to mitigate this behavior through instructions in the request, but OpenAI’s suggested intervention proved less effective in the system prompt. This compression saves tokens, with most of the token savings coming from dropping spaces before numbers. I work, as many do, in a system that allows agents to talk to each other as well as to me.

Solomonoff induction with reflective oracles

LessWrong · 2026-11-19 04:36 UTC

Linkpost for https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14454v1 Our PIBBSS fellow Damini Kusum wrote an excellent paper on prediction with reflective oracle Solomonoff Induction (rOSI). Reflective oracles are best known for their game-theoretic applications, where they are often dismissed because "why would all players choose the same reflective oracle?" It turns out that reflective oracles can also be used to construct a version of Solomonoff induction (called rOSI) with very nice sequence prediction properties - roughly speaking, it can learn to extract computable structure from (partly) uncomputable sequences. In fact, its properties are quite reminiscent of logical induction, but this paper is much shorter and more accessible. In this context, there is only one "player" to choose an oracle, which is just a fixed-point (though you can sort of consider the set of hypotheses entertained by that player as subplayers who share the oracle). I think this paper is the clearest exposition of a very neat but previously obscure idea in agent foundations: self-reflection can overcome unrealizability.

Fried cheese is tasty, and cheese and apples go well together. I got excited about the idea of making some kind of cheesy-apple fritter, played around with a few things, and ended up with something I like a lot. If you just want the recipe, it's here. The short version is that you mix grated apple and cheese, with some potato and 'egg' for structure. For the egg I'm using precision-fermented egg whites, reconstituted with the juice from the apple (about 1/2 C) instead of water. This is a trick I want to play with more, since it allows you to get more flavor into a dish without reducing the liquid. The potato needs to cook more than everything else so I microwave it. Then I combine the potato (warm) and apple (cold) before adding cheese, so the cheese doesn't prematurely melt. Here's the potato and apple shreds: Mixing in the flour, 'egg', and cheese: Cook one side on medium heat until browned, then flip: Too hot and the cheese gets bitter; too cold and the cheese doesn't brown or crisp. Recently, Anthropic shared Anvil, a system that uses Claude to autonomously search for jailbreaks in their models and design better safeguards. Inspired by Anvil, we propose that a frontier agent could autonomously improve the general safety of another model. Borrowing a term from cybersecurity, we use blue-teaming as a descriptive name for this process. More broadly, we wanted to explore whether tasks like these could become environments in which agents learn to do AI Safety research. Figure 1. A blue-teaming loop. Prior work has explored agent-driven safety improvements. Anthropic’s A3 addresses safety concerns via SFT data generation and fine-tuning within a predefined pipeline. Our experiment places greater emphasis on safety research as a hill-climbable task environment, where general-purpose frontier coding agents can iteratively design interventions. Rebliteration In our experiment, we tasked GPT 6.1 Sol (xhigh) with improving the safety of an abliterated variant of Gemma 4 12B, while maintaining useful behavior. We call this process "rebliteration".

Evaluation Awareness is Probably Distorting Monitor Evaluations

LessWrong · 2026-11-19 00:34 UTC

TL;DR: Monitors do worse on monitoring evaluations when they verbalize evaluation awareness in their transcripts. We ran four models as monitors on agent transcripts from two state-of-the-art monitor benchmarks. In over 22K monitor reviews, almost a quarter of the monitors verbalized evaluation awareness. Comparing the different conclusions the monitors reached following their verbalized awareness, we show that monitors will flag fewer harmful actions, and more honest transcripts. Introduction Monitoring systems play a central part in the AI Control agenda and in all frontier labs’ safety plans. Preventing incidents caused by misaligned or misused models requires reliable systems for detecting potential harm. Currently, frontier lab monitoring systems rely heavily on models, because it is hard to monitor AI agents using deterministic techniques. AI labs test their monitors using monitor evals. However, strong models have the capability to know when they are being evaluated. Evaluation awareness in models has become a central challenge and shows up consistently in model cards.

How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day

Big Think · 2026-11-18 07:00 UTC

As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now take more than a full day for that signal to arrive. At that impressive distance, more than three times the distance to Pluto, over 16 billion miles, and over 25.9 billion kilometers away, the Sun appears 30,000 times fainter than it does from Earth. (That’s still brighter than the full Moon, but only by a factor of 14, or under three astronomical magnitudes.) It’s moving away from the Sun at a current speed of 60,770 km/hr (37,760 mph), and has reached that one light-day milestone after a cumulative journey of 49 years and 72 days. In all the years since 1977, we’ve never launched another spacecraft that has rivaled Voyager 1. No other spacecraft has traveled as far; no other spacecraft is leaving the Solar System with as rapid a velocity; no current or even planned spacecraft is on track to ever overtake it.

8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic

Big Think · 2026-11-17 07:00 UTC

Here in this Universe, there are multiple different ways to look at all that exists in terms of size. You can look at the physical size, or volumes, that the objects occupy, and you can do that in a variety of ways. For humans, we can measure our dimensions — things like our height, width, and depth — or the amount of volume we displace when placed in a bath of water. Whichever method we choose, we get a proxy for our size. For planets, we can look at the edges of their solid surfaces or atmospheres; for stars, we can look at the boundary of their photospheres; for atoms, we probe them through techniques like force microscopy or scattering experiments. But in addition to these physical sizes, we can also examine such objects relative to other objects of the same type as found in nature. We can look at the distance from one human to another, for example, under a variety of common conditions. We can examine the distances between atoms, or stars, or planets, or galaxies, or anything else that we choose.

Scene Report | Summer Break in Mexico City

MUBI Notebook · 2026-11-16 08:00 UTC

Scene Report is a series that explores a city's moviegoing culture over a month. Illustration by Angelo Dolojan. There are summers when Mexico City belongs to cinema. This was not one of them—it belonged to football. Months before the first whistle, sidewalks were being repaired with unusual urgency, facades were being repainted, metro stations acquired new signage, long-neglected public spaces suddenly became worthy of investment. Like every global mega-event, the FIFA World Cup arrived with the familiar rhetoric of urban renewal and international prestige. Whether those promises will outlast the tournament remains to be seen. What mattered during those weeks was that the city had accepted football as its temporary organizing principle. As someone who had deliberately decided to stay in Mexico City to experience the tournament, I surrendered without resistance. I have always loved football, and the chance to watch a World Cup unfold in my own city felt like a once-in-a-lifetime experience. During the tournament, everyday routines dissolved into celebration.

Federico Luis is an Argentine filmmaker who has directed nearly ten documentary and fiction short films. In 2019, he presented La siesta in the Official Short Film Competition at the Cannes Film Festival, a section he recently returned to, winning the Palme d’Or for his documentary Para los contrincantes (2026), filmed in Mexico. In 2024, he premiered his debut feature, Simon of the Mountain, at Cannes Critics’ Week, where it received the Grand Prize. The film subsequently screened at several other international festivals, including San Sebastián, Havana, Cairo and Biarritz. Through a filmography that, in different ways, unsettles, distorts and expands reality, Luis explores how the freedom of fantasy can lend an air of mystery to the most ordinary situations.

Our new season about dissident filmmakers kicks off with the tale of Yilmaz Güney—one of Turkish cinema’s most revered and controversial directors—from his days as a tough-guy movie star nicknamed “The Ugly King,” to his years as a left-wing activist, to his 19-year prison sentence…during which he somehow managed to make his masterpiece, Yol (1982). Featuring Oscar-winner and Yol megafan Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Digger, 2026) and German-Turkish auteur Fatih Akin (Head-On, 2004). The MUBI Podcast returns for its 12th season, “Under Pressure.” At a time when artists worldwide are being threatened or stifled by their governments, host Rico Gagliano tells the stories of filmmakers from across history and around the world who have made movies in spite of incredible state pressure to compromise, give in, or give up. From 1970s Turkey to modern-day America, these are alternately wild, sobering, controversial, and inspiring tales of art by any means necessary.

To accompany his Unlimited Editions report in The Wire 514, Tim Fish compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Liverpool label When Blah Records emerged into the UK’s hiphop landscape in 2006, they formed part of an alternative movement to a rather dominant London scene. Co-founded by Lee Scott and Alex Jennings (aka Molotov), the label was primarily a way to officially distribute music for the rap crew Children Of The Damned (COTD), and the majority of artists who have put out records on the label over the subsequent 20 years have all had some real-life connection to Scott. The following playlist outlines some of Blah's most significant records. Children Of The Damned “Cold Sag Run Marathon” From Brick Pelican (2009) Children Of The Damned were the original Blah artists and they still remain at the core of the label today, albeit with expanded numbers and a slightly different name. This track gives a flavour of their origins and an even better indicator of how much their sound has evolved.

Mark Korven: Borderline Sonics and Dimensional Demarcation

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-16 00:00 UTC

Mark Korven’s scores for The Black Phone (2021) and Them (2021) destabilise hermetic soundworlds to convey psychological violence, writes Philip Brophy in his latest Secret History of Film Music column The contribution of Canadian composer Mark Korven to contemporary horror cinema is aligned with composers who sculpt their scores through tactile manipulation. His self-built Apprehension Engine, a hybrid guitar-percussion instrument, empowers distinctive acoustic control. Korven commissioned Toronto based guitar maker Tony Duggan-Smith to build the modest box incorporating tools and techniques favoured by Korven: a hurdy-gurdy for cranking, a spring reverb for metallic resonance, metal rods and wooden tongues for bowing (similar to the waterphone), and a stretched wire for E-bowing. Its abject sonics pepper Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse (2019) with terse shudders and emotional spikes, and are also audible in Adam Schindler and Brian Netto’s Don’t Move (2024).

Global Ear: Colombo

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-12 00:00 UTC

To accompany his Global Ear feature in The Wire 514, Simon Coates compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Sri Lankan city Situated on Colombo’s Vauxhall Street, Musicmatters sits at the centre of the Sri Lankan city's experimental music world. “A lot of my introduction to experimentation in music came through Musicmatters around 2010,” says bass player Uvindu Perera. “I was new to it then, but these people were already listening widely and sharing references.” Simultaneously a collective, a school (Perera now teaches there), a record label and home to the Sound Room performance space, Musicmatters offers both an alternative to exam-heavy Western music education and provides space for explorations in sound as art and experimentation. Many of the musicians in this playlist have links to the organisation. Video: ZeN's Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital concert, Istanbul, 1998

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-10 00:00 UTC

Watch an exclusive clip of Turkish improv band ZeN’s Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital concert from 1998 On 23 June 1998, Istanbul based experimental rock group ZeN performed at Bakırköy Psychiatric Hospital, following an invitation from two nurses who worked there. The musicians visited the hospital beforehand and decided to approach the performance with sensitivity to their audience while remaining true to their commitment to improvisation. At times, the lyrics seem to tell the story of the hospital and the concert itself, responding directly to the surroundings. The performance subsequently became one of the group’s most remarkable and cult recordings, released on cassette and CD in 1999 and reissued on vinyl in 2023. This exclusive edit with English subtitles is hosted by The Wire ahead of the release of a new documentary, ZeNistan, exploring the activities of ZeN throughout the 1990s.

culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Against the Grain: Music criticism can become critical again – here's how

The Wire Magazine · 2026-11-09 00:00 UTC

Popular music criticism can become relevant again by situating itself in broader theoretical frameworks, argues Rafael Lubner in The Wire 514 These are lean times for popular music criticism. Negotiating a gutted publishing landscape, amid a Spotify-led devaluation of listening, the form finds itself under serious threat. One index of criticism’s attenuated state is the narrowing frame of reference employed by critics to apprehend musical objects – rarely do we find new works in the visual arts, film or literature employed to understand transformations in music’s sound or form. Take, as a point of comparison, Greg Tate’s recently reissued Flyboy In The Buttermilk (reviewed in The Wire 513). Here are passionate defences of Miles Davis’s earth-shaking mid-1970s funk odysseys alongside surveys of Afrodiasporic art and reviews of writer Nathaniel Mackey and literary critic Henry Louis Gates Jr. Contemporary music criticism, by contrast, seems resolutely committed to understanding music as siloed from the non-musical.

World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

Rock Paper Shotgun · 2026-11-18 17:44 UTC

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning. Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019.

Rock Paper Shotgun · 2026-11-18 16:16 UTC

At this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container. A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6's idolising reviews, that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?

journal · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Thermodynamic Parameterizations of Dark Energy in Light of DESI DR2 BAO

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The physical origin of cosmic acceleration remains one of the central unresolved problems of modern cosmology. Although the $\Lambda$CDM model successfully describes a wide range of cosmological observations, its interpretation in terms of a strictly constant vacuum energy faces long-standing theoretical challenges, motivating the search for physically grounded alternatives. In this work, we develop a thermodynamic parametrization of dark energy (TPDE) by combining the second law of thermodynamics with the kinematic evolution of the Universe. By imposing physically motivated constraints on the cosmic deceleration parameter and reconstructing its evolution through a Pad\'e approximant, we derive a one-parameter extension of $\Lambda$CDM in which late-time accelerated expansion emerges from thermodynamic principles rather than an assumed cosmological constant.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Effect of scrape-off losses and current flattening on runaway electron dynamics in ARC

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disruptions in high-current tokamaks, such as ARC, may result in megaampere-scale runaway electron currents. In this work, we evaluate mitigation strategies via massive material injection, accounting for the combined impact of scrape-off losses due to vertical displacement events and current profile relaxation during the thermal quench. We find that scrape-off losses alone yield only modest reductions in runaway electron currents, but combining them with current flattening creates a beneficial synergistic effect. The latter broadens the current channel outward, shifting efficient runaway electron generation closer to the plasma edge where the dynamically contracting boundary can effectively scrape off the electron beams. This interplay significantly expands the operational window for mitigation toward lower assimilated densities, theoretically reducing runaway currents to manageable levels at experimentally feasible assimilated quantities.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45{\deg}N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Dynamic Vacuum Energy in Weyl Integrable Spacetime Part I: Implications for Inflationary Cosmology

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explore a dynamic vacuum energy scenario within the Weyl Integrable Spacetime (WIS) framework and provide the Friedmann--Lema\^itre (FL) cosmology equations under a metric endowed with a lapse function. We pay particular attention to the implications of inflationary dynamics. We show that the explicit vacuum decay source cancels in the FL acceleration equation, where the Hubble slow-roll parameter is controlled by the non-vacuum sector alone, while the dynamic vacuum defined in proper time $\Lambda(\tau)$ itself continues to enter the observables through the expansion rate. We identify the warm inflation (WI) dissipation coefficient with one half of the logarithmic decay rate of the vacuum energy, $\Upsilon=-\tfrac{1}{2} d\ln\Lambda/d\tau$, hence the phenomenological friction coefficient is tied to the vacuum sector rather than computed from explicit inflaton--bath microphysics.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter of the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider

arXiv · 2026-11-19 05:00 UTC

arXiv:2611.23457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a next-generation facility expected to address fundamental open questions in nuclear physics, including the structure and dynamics of gluons in nucleons and nuclei. The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC) is the electromagnetic calorimeter of the ePIC detector, designed to meet the stringent performance requirements of the EIC, providing precise measurements and particle identification of scattered electrons, photons, and neutral mesons. The BIC is a high-granularity sampling calorimeter based on lead absorbers interleaved with scintillating fibers, complemented by pixelated imaging layers based on the AstroPix monolithic active pixel sensor. This hybrid design enables both accurate energy and position measurements, as well as three-dimensional shower reconstruction, making it a key component for realizing the full physics potential of the EIC. The BIC has successfully completed its Preliminary Design Review last year and is currently progressing toward the Final Design Review.

preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

The vitamin D-vitamin D receptor axis in uterine leiomyomas: A scoping review of clinical, molecular, and genetic evidence

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Godfrey Katamba, Rogers Kajabwangu, Hamson Kanyesigye, Mivule A. Kinene, David Collins Agaba, Ronald Ouma Omolo, Agnes Namaganda, Haruna Muwonge Uterine leiomyomas are the most common benign tumours of the female reproductive tract and a major cause of gynaecological morbidity worldwide. Observational and experimental studies have linked vitamin D and the vitamin D receptor (VDR) separately to uterine leiomyoma biology, including effects on cell proliferation and Wnt/β-catenin signalling in vitro; however, the breadth of this evidence has not been comprehensively mapped across clinical, molecular, and genetic domains. We conducted a scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched from January 2016 to December 2025. Forty-two studies were included: 31 clinical, seven molecular, and four genetic.

journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Social support networks of older adults before, during and after the COVID-19 pandemic

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Marjan Cugmas, Anuška Ferligoj, Tina Kogovšek, Zenel Batagelj Societies are considerably challenged by population aging, especially when it comes to providing services and support for older adults. Although formal services such as home care and volunteering address some of these needs, the informal social support given by relatives, friends and neighbours is just as vital. In Slovenia, the share of older adults reporting they have no informal social support rose from around 1% in 2002 to 7.8% in 2020, coinciding with the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. The article examines the prevalence and characteristics of social support network types relied on by older adults in Slovenia between 2002 and 2025, with a special focus on the post-pandemic recovery. To that end, a cross-sectional survey collected ego-centred network data of older adults (65+) in Slovenia in 2002, 2020 and 2025. The samples are representative of both gender and region. The data were analysed using clustering for symbolic data and correspondence analysis.

Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology among football players in Africa: A systematic review of injury incidence, patterns and associated factors

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Fadilulahi Adekilekun Jimoh, Adeola Medinat Adepoju, Samuel Timileyin Afolabi, Abass Mosebolatan Bolarinwa Background Football is widely played across Africa, yet evidence on the epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries among African football players remains fragmented across countries, populations, and competitive settings. Differences in injury definitions, surveillance methods, and exposure measurement further limit comparison between studies. This systematic review synthesised the available evidence on musculoskeletal injury epidemiology in African football. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by backward citation searching. Studies investigating musculoskeletal injuries among football players in Africa were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer.

Analysis of the biological characteristics and gene function of <i>Lactobacillus delbrueckii</i> subsp. <i>sunkii</i>

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Yi Wu, Chunlei Zhang, Mengjie Luo, Feng Hai, Xianhua Liu, Xian Jin The biological characteristics, morphology, and genomic information of Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. sunkii, isolated from the vaginal secretions of pregnant women, have not yet been reported. Elucidating its biological properties and genetic functions may provide a theoretical foundation for developing probiotic preparations to treat bacterial vaginosis. The strain was identified as L. delbrueckii subsp. sunkii using mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) gene sequencing. Colony morphology was observed, Gram staining characteristics were examined, and cellular ultrastructure was visualized via scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Whole-genome sequencing was performed using both second- and third-generation sequencing platforms, followed by comprehensive bioinformatics analysis. Additionally, biochemical experiments, H2O2 production tests, acid production assays, antibacterial activity assays, and antimicrobial susceptibility tests were conducted.

X-band near-perfect absorber based on electromagnetic metasurface

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Changliang Lin, Hanhui Wang, Kaitong Wang, Xiong Wang, Gongnan Li The development of compact, miniaturized absorbers in the microwave band is of great significance for enhancing the performance of small aerial platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles. Conventional absorbers typically rely on materials with specific thicknesses or on active components, which limits their applicability in practical scenarios. To address these issues, this work proposes a metasurface-based approach in which dipole resonances are engineered to achieve impedance matching, realizing a maximum absorptance of 99.6% at 10 GHz for optimized device. At the same time, the absorber maintains an absorptance above 50% for incidence angles ranging from 0° to 70°. Finite-element simulations are employed to elucidate the physical origin of the absorption and the impact of varying structural parameters.

Theorising research publication practices among African university-based researchers

PLOS ONE Biology · 2026-11-18 14:00 UTC

by Meshack Nzesei Mutua, Felix Otieno, Marthe Montcho, Ferdinand C. Mukumbang Understanding research publication practices among African academics is critical to promoting knowledge equity and addressing structural and systemic challenges that disproportionately affect them, thereby increasing the quantity and quality of scientific output and catalysing socio-economic development on the continent. By exploring research publication practices among university-based African researchers, this paper offers transferable insights into how and why initiatives can promote positive publication practices, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Using an Indigenous realist evaluation approach, data were collected from three distinct African research project teams that participated in research capacity-strengthening workshops to enhance their research publication skills. Nineteen (19) interviews with the Principal Investigators and other collaborating researchers were conducted.

The report, Open Science and the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Exchange: Policy Options for Reliable Research,1 published in October, 2026, was commissioned by the European Parliament's Panel for the Future of Science and Technology at a crucial moment for research. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how knowledge is created2 as AI systems are increasingly integrated across many stages of the research lifecycle.3 These methodological and epistemological challenges are leading to AI capabilities that now outpace human verification, transforming scientific disciplines faster than researchers or current governance can respond.

[Editorial] Health and poverty: lessons from China

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

The world has never been wealthier. Yet in 2025, an estimated 831 million people lived on less than US$3 per day. This stark disparity exposes a systemic failure to translate global prosperity into basic security and opportunity for all. As slowing economic growth and multiple crises, such as conflict and climate change, undermine the momentum of global poverty reduction, governments now face a pressing test: whether they will still find, reach, and protect those already furthest behind, or allow them to fall deeper into poverty.

Geopolitical conflict, faltering multilateralism, and economic factors such as inflation have made it more challenging to address global poverty eradication and health goals. The relationship between health and poverty has long been recognised, yet policy responses often remain fragmented.

The Lancet · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Poverty alleviation is a pressing global challenge that is intricately linked with health, as emphasised by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In 2019, out-of-pocket health expenditure—health-care costs paid directly by individuals or households rather than covered by insurance or other third-party payers—pushed an additional 344 million people into poverty globally. In 2020, 724 million people were living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than US$2·15 per person per day at 2017 purchasing power parity, 90 million more than the pre-COVID-19 pandemic UN projection.

Catching AI's Mistakes Has a Real Cost

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

remote_worker writes: A look at the difference in effort, understanding, and recall between creating something versus verifying it, and the human tendencies towards verifying things. https://theconversation.com/catching-ais-mistakes-is-a-mental-burden-and-a-drag-on-productivity-291748 By now, almost everyone has asked an AI agent a question, only to realize that the answer seems not quite right. Something might be missing or wrong or out of date. An executive assistant told me she uses AI tools for drafting itineraries and briefings, but she's caught enough issues that she now builds time into her workflow to thoroughly check for inaccuracies and biases. Therein lies the catch: AI responses can improve productivity, but the gains are often countered by time and mental energy spent determining whether the output is accurate and appropriate. This is the verification burden. Sometimes the cost is worth it, sometimes it isn't. Original Submission Read more of this story at SoylentNews.

ULA Vulcan Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: It's the alliance's first launch failure since it formed in 2006: United Launch Alliance is known for its ultra-dependable Atlas V, but its its latest rocket is off to a sputtering start. The new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket malfunctioned while climbing into space yesterday, destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the company said in a post on X. "We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible." Launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the company formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable.

datasette-arrows 0.1a0

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-18 17:09 UTC

Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette, projects

specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

NGINX2Root: Remote Code Execution vulnerabilities in nginx

LWN.net · 2026-11-18 16:13 UTC

Xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The company also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available. We also obtained a root shell on the host in a setup where nginx was running in a Docker container. On many Linux distributions, the SCTP module is installed by default and the kernel loads it automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket. Whether SCTP is reachable on a given host still depends on the kernel, the available modules, and the container's restrictions. Where it is reachable, the attacker can take over the host kernel.

Datacenters' Share of UK Planning Applications Nearly Triples in Three Years

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: Councils waving through majority of proposals as government turns on the AI-friendly planning taps: Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. [...] Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected.

Trump Admin Loses Fight to Spy on Random Journalists’ LinkedIn DMs

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Arthur t Knackerbracket writes: Confidential sources "lifeblood" of free press, court rules in LinkedIn fight: The Trump administration's fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can't sweep in "a vast number of confidential sources" of random journalists "who have no conceivable relationship" to the Department of Justice's investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.

The Latest FreeBSD Report is Here, and the AI Debate is Ongoing

SoylentNews · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

Arthur t Knackerbracket writes: Only a minority want to ban it: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space.

External sandboxes for coding agents

Simon Willison's Weblog · 2026-11-17 22:52 UTC

External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects. My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Bliki: Generated Glossary

Martin Fowler · Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知

When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job. The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion.

Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux

The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load. Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel.

Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-11-16 18:35 UTC

The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly. In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40.

Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap

Kubernetes Blog · 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics / IEEE Spectrum · 2026-11-16 14:00 UTC

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die. The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says.

28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-11-16 10:00 UTC

This article is brought to you by VicOne. VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations. What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited.

Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data-Scaling Problem?

IEEE Spectrum Robotics · 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC

Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question. Nobody knows how much data would be necessary, what kind of data is important, or whether something else might be missing. And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: The resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe.
